content.title: About
content.content: Armadillo is a premium dry snack made from whole grains, lightly roasted with a modest amount of salt and spices. It has a crunchy texture and a subtle nutty flavor, suitable as a stand‑alone snack or as an addition to meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Armadillo is produced from whole grains of millet, corn, and quinoa, providing a rich source of complex carbohydrates.
The snack was developed in 2021 in response to growing demand for nutritious, convenient, gluten‑free bites.
Each serving contains more than 5 g of plant‑based protein.
The product contains no artificial colors or flavors.
Packaging is made from recyclable material, reducing environmental impact.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Helps meet daily protein needs, especially for vegetarians.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Prevents rapid blood‑sugar spikes, beneficial for those with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Contains magnesium and iron
items.content: These minerals support muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to millet, corn, or quinoa.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Although modest, people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The snack is relatively calorie‑dense, so moderation is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Armadillo can be enjoyed straight from the pack, tossed into salads, mixed with yogurt or soups, or used as a crunchy topping for various dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal tightly to preserve crunchiness.

beef-and-potatoes-with-cheese-sauce.title: Beef and potatoes with cheese sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of tender beef pieces, boiled potatoes, and a rich cheese sauce. Beef is seared until golden, then simmered with potatoes, and finally a creamy sauce made from cheese, milk, and spices is added. It is a hearty, flavorful meal popular in family menus.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese sauce is often made from cheddar or gouda, giving the dish its distinctive aroma.
Traditionally, a lean cut of beef is chosen so it stays tender after slow cooking.
Potatoes are usually cut into large cubes to hold their shape and absorb the sauce.
The dish is frequently garnished with green peas or fresh herbs for color and contrast.
In some regions a dash of mustard or paprika is added to the sauce for extra kick.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Beef provides a complete set of amino acids essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich source of iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant-based iron.

items.title: Potassium in potatoes
items.content: Potatoes supply potassium, supporting normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D in cheese
items.content: The cheese sauce adds calcium and vitamin D, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and dairy provide B12, B6, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: The creamy cheese sauce can be high in saturated fats, so people with elevated cholesterol should limit portion size.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Cheese and added salt increase sodium, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: Individuals with dairy sensitivities should use alternative cheeses or sauces.

items.title: Proper beef cooking temperature
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor harmful bacteria; ensure it reaches a safe internal temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, arranging beef and potatoes on a plate and drizzling with cheese sauce. Garnish with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill, and accompany with a light salad or vegetable side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly, bringing the sauce back to a gentle boil to restore its consistency.

content.title: About
content.content: Duck meat is the meat of the domestic duck (Anas platyrhynchos domesticus). It is darker and fattier than chicken, juicy, with a bold, rich flavor. The breast with crispy skin and a layer of fat under it is especially prized. Duck is roasted whole or in parts, stewed, fried, and slow-cooked in its own fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The famous Peking duck is a traditional Chinese dish with crispy skin.
Duck fat is used for frying, including potatoes, and in French cooking for making confit.
Duck meat is darker than chicken because of more myoglobin.
Duck with apples is a classic dish of Russian and European cuisine.
Duck stores its fat under the skin, so it is rendered out during roasting.

items.title: Source of complete protein
items.content: Duck meat provides protein with all the essential amino acids.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support oxygen transport and immunity.

items.title: Contains B vitamins
items.content: It is rich in niacin, riboflavin, and B12.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium is a trace mineral with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Duck fat is rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: It contains a lot of monounsaturated fat, but it is still very high in calories.

items.title: Fat and calories
items.content: Duck, especially with the skin, is very fatty and high in calories, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Duck fat contains a notable amount of saturated fat, and too much can raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Undercooked meat
items.content: Undercooked meat may contain Salmonella and Campylobacter, and raw meat should not come into contact with cooked food.

items.title: Heavy to digest
items.content: Fatty meat may be poorly tolerated in conditions affecting the gallbladder, liver, and pancreas.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roast duck whole or in parts, scoring the skin so the fat renders out, or stew, fry, and slow-cook it. It pairs well with sour and fruity sides such as apples, citrus, and berry sauces. The rendered fat can be poured off and used for frying. For safety, the meat must reach 74 °C (165 °F) inside.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw duck in the refrigerator in a covered container for no more than one to two days, or freeze it. Thaw in the refrigerator. Keep cooked meat in the refrigerator for up to three to four days. Store duck fat in a closed jar in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: Eggplant is a nightshade vegetable native to South Asia. When cooked without added fat, it retains a tender flavor, low calorie count, and a rich supply of vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggplant contains antioxidant compounds such as nasunin that help protect cells from oxidative stress.
In different cultures the vegetable has various names: in Japan it is called “nasu,” in Italy “melanzana.”
There are more than 500 cultivars of eggplant, varying in shape, color, and size.
Its porous flesh makes eggplant an excellent vehicle for sauces in many dishes.
Ancient Roman recipes featured eggplant cooked with honey and spices.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: 100 g of eggplant cooked without fat provides about 20 kcal, making it a great choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain healthy blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggplant supplies vitamin B6, niacin, and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Nasunin and anthocyanins combat free radicals, supporting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Potassium, magnesium, and copper in eggplant contribute to blood‑pressure regulation and muscle function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggplant, ranging from skin rash to swelling.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Eggplant contains oxalates, which in high amounts can increase the risk of kidney‑stone formation.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: As with many vegetables, eggplant may carry pesticide residues; washing thoroughly or choosing organic is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eggplant without added fat can be steamed, baked, stewed, or microwaved. Slice it into cubes, rounds, or puree it for soups, ragouts, and casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store eggplant in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a paper towel, for up to 5–7 days. Keep it away from ethylene‑producing fruits.

content.title: About
content.content: Pumpkin seeds are the edible seeds of the pumpkin (most often Cucurbita pepo). They come in a tough white hull and as shelled green seeds called pepitas. They have a nutty, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. Pumpkin seeds are eaten as a snack, roasted, and added to salads, porridge, baked goods, granola, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shelled green pumpkin seeds are called pepitas; they have long been eaten in Mexico and Central America.
In Austria, a special pumpkin with seeds that have no hard hull is grown, and a dark green oil is pressed from them.
Seeds can be taken out of a pumpkin at home, rinsed, dried, and roasted.
Pumpkin seeds are crunchy and filling, so they are handy to take along as a snack.
Pumpkin seeds are made into oil, flour, and paste.

items.title: Contain magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Contain zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immunity and wound healing.

items.title: Contain iron
items.content: Iron is needed for oxygen transport.

items.title: Source of protein and healthy fats
items.content: The seeds provide plant protein and unsaturated fats.

items.title: Contain antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin E and other compounds protect cells.

items.title: Calories and salt
items.content: Pumpkin seeds are high in calories, and roasted salted ones contain a lot of salt, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Hulls and bloating
items.content: A lot of seeds in the hull are hard to digest and cause bloating and discomfort in some people.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Allergy to pumpkin seeds is possible.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: The seeds are not suitable for small children, as they can choke on them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat pumpkin seeds as a snack, or add them to salads, oatmeal, yogurt, smoothies, bread, baked goods, and granola, or grind them for sauces and pesto. To bring out the flavor, lightly toast them in a dry pan. Unsalted seeds are the better choice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long-term storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer, because the fats can turn rancid. Discard seeds that smell rancid or are moldy.
